title: One Dollar or Twenty
text:
In 1959 Leon Festinger and James Carlsmith of Stanford University gave male students an hour of deliberately boring work. First they loaded spools onto a tray, emptied it and loaded it again. Then they turned square pegs on a board a quarter turn at a time, over and over.

When the hour was up, the experimenter explained that his assistant had not shown up, and asked a favor. Would the student tell the next participant, a young woman waiting outside, that the tasks were interesting and enjoyable? Some students were offered one dollar for this, others twenty dollars, a considerable sum at the time. Almost all agreed and told her the tasks were fun. A control group did the tasks without being asked to say anything.

Later, in what seemed to be a separate interview, all the students were asked how much they had actually enjoyed the tasks. Those paid twenty dollars rated them about as dull as the control group did. Those paid only one dollar rated them as noticeably more enjoyable. Festinger explained this with his theory of cognitive dissonance. Twenty dollars was a good enough reason to tell a small lie. One dollar was not, so those students eased the discomfort of having lied by coming to believe it.
lesson: Small incentives can change what people believe, while big ones only change what they do. If you want real commitment, rely on persuasion and choice rather than heavy rewards.
source: Festinger, L., and Carlsmith, J. M. (1959). Cognitive consequences of forced compliance. Journal of Abnormal and Social Psychology, 58(2), 203-210.
